title: English Skill Lab – Listening Full Mock 04

parts.title: Booking a local film equipment kit

speakers.role: Little Quay Equipment Library employee: Nadia

turns.text_en: Hello, Little Quay Equipment Library, Nadia speaking. We have kits for sound, lighting and video, but the right set depends on what you're making. Some community groups reserve everything and then discover they've borrowed more than they can carry. Can you tell me about the project and who'll be operating the equipment?

We're making a short documentary about the old shopping street. It's for a neighbourhood screening, not a commercial project, and our volunteers know basic camera work but have never borrowed sound equipment from you.
It's a documentary, mainly short interviews with long-term shopkeepers. We considered doing a fictional drama, but we don't have actors or time to rehearse scenes.
A documentary is quite suitable for our basic kit. Most of your sound challenges will probably involve traffic rather than complicated studio effects.
We thought a large microphone on a stand would be the safest choice, but the shopkeepers will often be moving around behind their counters.
A lapel microphone is better in that situation because it follows the speaker. We'll show you how to attach it without rubbing against clothing.
One camera could capture everything, but we'd like a second angle for interviews so we don't have to ask busy people to repeat their answers.
I'll reserve two cameras. They can be matched for colour, which saves considerable time when you edit the footage.
Our first interview is on Wednesday afternoon. We hoped to collect the kit on Monday, but the person who drives our van is unavailable until Tuesday.
Tuesday collection is fine. We'll keep the equipment together, so you can check the contents before leaving.
One volunteer offered to watch a video at home, but do we need to attend anything in person before taking the lights?
Everyone handling the lighting stands must attend our safety briefing. It's short, but it's essential because the stands can fall if they aren't weighted correctly.

One more point concerns data safety. Please make two copies of your recordings before returning any storage cards. Our staff do not keep backup versions of clients' projects, and the cards are erased as part of the next equipment preparation cycle.

Thanks for making that clear. We have a portable drive and access to a secure shared folder, so we can copy the material at the end of each filming day. I will also ask somebody other than the camera operator to check that the files actually open.

During the recording demonstration, we also show how to keep a brief log of each interview. You can note the subject, the time and whether the participant has agreed to be recorded. That prevents confusion when several files have similar names.

We hadn't planned a log, but I can see how useful it would be. The shops are quite noisy, and we may need to repeat an answer after a lorry passes. A written note would help us find the best recording later without listening to every file from the beginning.
I saw a poster showing a forty-pound deposit, and our treasurer set aside that amount. Has the policy changed since the library added new cameras?
The refundable deposit is sixty-five pounds. It is returned after the kit is checked, provided nothing is missing or broken.
We're filming Thursday and Friday. Could we bring everything back on Saturday morning? We don't want to rush the last interview just to meet a Friday deadline.
Saturday works. Please return the batteries fully charged so the next group can test everything promptly.
Will we have to bring our own tripod? The group has a very old one, and one of its legs is no longer secure.
A tripod is included with each camera. You can leave the damaged one at home; we'd rather you used a stable support.
Our editor asked whether we should record compressed audio to save space. We have enough storage, so quality is more important than very small files.
Record the interviews as WAV files. They'll take more space, but they're easier to process without adding another layer of compression.
Can any volunteer collect it, or does the person whose name is on the booking have to appear? The group might arrive in two separate cars.
The team leader must sign for the kit. Other members can help carry it, but responsibility needs to be clear.

We'll place a numbered checklist inside every case. If you notice a missing cable or a scratched lens, please tell the counter staff before you leave. That simple check protects your group as well as the equipment library.

I'll brief our team leader before collection and ask everyone to check the cases while we're still at the desk. We won't know whether the footage is usable until later, so I'd rather prevent a missing cable or flat battery now. Thanks for taking us through it.

questions.explanation_vi: **Đáp án đúng: A – the team's appointed leader.** Câu hỏi: Who signs for the kit at collection? **Evidence (T25, T26):** “Can any volunteer collect it, or does the person whose name is on the booking have to appear? The group might arrive in two separate cars. The team leader must sign for the kit. Other members can help carry it, but responsibility needs to be clear.”. parts.title: A Day at the Hill Railway Heritage Site

turns.text_en: Welcome to the Hill Railway Heritage Site. I'm Ellis, the visitor manager. Take out today's plan rather than the leaflet you may have seen online: several displays moved during the restoration work. The entrance is at the bottom of the page, the former track is along the northern edge, and the information point is close to the courtyard. No demonstration train will move today, but the trackside safety line still applies. I'll talk you through the route before we set off.

The signal house is the small building directly north of the central courtyard, just before the railway track. On your map this is the upper middle space, not the room by the entrance. Inside you'll see the old levers that directed trains between tracks. A volunteer explains why pulling the wrong lever could cause a serious conflict on a busy line.

The children's carriage stands on the central southern spur, between the main entrance and the courtyard. It is the covered carriage with steps designed for younger visitors. The larger passenger coach beside the main track is closed for repairs. Families should use the southern carriage because its interior has been adapted for safe, supervised handling of historic objects.

The steam workshop is halfway up the western side of the grounds. Walk from the courtyard towards the left-hand service path and stop before the northern track; don't continue to the far north-west corner. The workshop has a broad brick chimney. Staff explain how old engines were cleaned and inspected, but the machinery isn't operated while visitors are inside.

The viewing platform is in the north-east corner, at the far right end of the track. From there visitors can see the curve of the line beyond the station. It is not the low balcony outside the café. Please use the staircase and handrail rather than climbing the earth bank, which is especially slippery after heavy rain.

The refreshment kiosk stands near the entrance on the south-west side. People sometimes walk towards the north-east platform thinking the café is there, but refreshments are sold close to the main gate. The kiosk serves simple hot drinks and sandwiches, and it has a sheltered seating area where groups can wait for the next tour.

The engineering demonstration begins at thirteen forty. The timetable lists a staff-only equipment check at one fifteen, so please don't confuse the two activities. We allow visitors into the demonstration zone only after safety barriers have been checked. The talk covers how pressure was monitored in historic boilers, using models rather than a working steam engine.

Visitors entering the practical workshop need green tickets. General admission tickets are white and don't include that activity, while orange tags belong to the volunteer team. If you haven't booked a workshop place, ask at the information point; any spare spaces will be allocated there, not by the workshop door.

Photography is not allowed in the archive room. Staff are happy to describe the collection, and you may make handwritten notes, but some documents are too fragile for repeated exposure to bright light. Copies of selected images can be requested afterwards through the archive team. Please don't assume a phone camera is harmless simply because it has a small flash.

The iron footbridge beyond the northern track is awaiting repair. The main pedestrian paths remain open, but nobody can cross the bridge until engineers have replaced damaged sections. The closure doesn't prevent access to the viewing platform: follow the eastern path instead and listen for instructions from the volunteers managing the crossing points.

Before you leave, please complete a feedback card at the exit. It asks which display helped you understand the railway's history and what remained confusing. We read the responses when planning new exhibits; the cards are anonymous, and there's no need to give your email address unless you'd like updates about future events.

You can spend longer at a particular exhibit, provided you remain on the marked visitor loop. If a sign is hard to read, please tell us rather than crossing the barrier for a closer look. Before leaving, return your headphones to the information point. It's the stories of the workers, as much as the machinery, that explain why this railway mattered locally.

parts.topic: Heritage railway museum and site tour

parts.title: Designing an Accessible Museum Tour
parts.context: academic discussion among students and tutor

turns.text_en: The museum has asked your group to evaluate an accessible guided tour. Please don't start with an assumption that one format works for every visitor. We want to understand barriers at different points in the visit and find out which changes people themselves say are useful.
We walked the route last week and recorded where the lighting changes, but we haven't yet involved visitors who use different access services. That is an obvious gap.
And the museum's old feedback form mostly asks whether people enjoyed the exhibition. It doesn't tell us when they couldn't follow an explanation or move between rooms.
Imagine two visitors who need very different ways to explore the exhibition. Before we order more equipment, how will you decide what they actually need?
Visitor choice is the essential principle. People should be able to select a route and information format that fits their needs instead of being given one mandatory solution.
We can test a small menu of formats and ask people what felt useful rather than ranking visitors by their abilities.
Your route notes mention a problem before the textile gallery. Was the corridor too narrow?
The main issue was the lighting transition. Visitors leave a bright space and enter a darker one almost immediately, with no time for their eyes to adjust.
That could affect navigation even when signs are large enough. We should look at lighting and wayfinding together.
You're planning to film reactions during the pilot. What permission must people provide before that happens?
They must give consent. We shouldn't assume that entering a museum means accepting research or being recorded for a student project.
We'll offer participation without filming and explain clearly how data will be used and stored.
Some visitors stopped asking questions halfway through. Did they lose interest, or could something else explain it?
The guide's pacing was too fast. People were still looking at one object when the talk moved to the next, so they had to choose between seeing and listening.
We can leave more time at key objects and put optional detail in a separate resource.
Your draft proposes another fifteen signs. Are you certain adding text is the best response to differing energy levels?
Route flexibility seems more useful. A shorter loop with clearly marked rest points might make the visit easier without adding visual clutter.
Let's test both route options and ask participants which they could complete comfortably.
A tactile model could let visitors explore the shape of one delicate sculpture without touching the original. It should be designed with museum conservators and people who use tactile information.
I'll ask which features are meaningful to include, rather than making an overly complicated copy of every surface detail.
And we should explain that the model is an interpretation, not an identical substitute for the original.
Use a captioned video for the short film in the final gallery. A printed transcript may help too, but it doesn't show how words align with the moving image.
We'll review caption timing and identify any relevant non-speech sounds rather than simply running speech recognition and assuming it's perfect.
That review should happen before the public trial, because poor captions can create new barriers.
A quiet session with fewer people and reduced background sound would allow us to test whether crowding is part of the problem.
We should announce the conditions accurately so visitors don't arrive expecting complete silence, which we can't guarantee in a public building.
And participation needs to remain voluntary; a separate time slot should not become the only way to access the museum.
A floor map showing lifts, rest points and exits would help visitors plan before arriving. It should also be available in formats that work with screen readers.
I'll make sure the map distinguishes actual step-free access from a route that merely looks short on paper.
We'll verify it on the ground with staff, not rely on an architectural drawing that may be out of date.
Finish with a feedback interview, rather than relying solely on a five-point satisfaction score. We need to know what worked and what remained difficult.
I'll use open questions and avoid asking participants to speak on behalf of everyone with similar access needs.
Then we can report varied experiences honestly and recommend further testing before a permanent redesign.
A good evaluation doesn't simply produce a list of features. It explains who benefited, where uncertainty remains and which changes the museum can maintain over time.
I'll revise our proposal to make participants' choice central, and I'll separate accessibility requirements from optional extras.
And I'll plan the pilot so we don't treat one favourable comment as proof that the whole route is accessible.

questions.prompt_en: What principle should guide the redesign?
questions.explanation_vi: **Đáp án A – visitors choosing their preferred route.** Nguyên tắc cốt lõi là để từng khách tham quan tự chọn lộ trình và kiểu thông tin phù hợp nhu cầu. **B – providing a larger supply of leaflets:** Tăng số tờ rơi không bảo đảm đáp ứng nhu cầu khác nhau; đoạn nói nhấn vào quyền chọn hình thức và tuyến. **C – using the most advanced equipment:** Nhóm được yêu cầu nghĩ về nhu cầu người dùng trước khi đặt thiết bị, không chạy theo thiết bị hiện đại nhất. **Bẫy nghe hiểu:** Visitor choice được nói dưới dạng select a route and information format. **Vị trí bằng chứng:** Part 3, lượt T04, T05, T06. *Lời giải biên tập; chưa được giáo viên xác nhận độc lập.*

questions.prompt_en: Which feature created a problem on the original route?
questions.explanation_vi:
**Đáp án A: a sudden brightness contrast.** Người xem đi từ phòng sáng sang chỗ tối quá nhanh, mắt chưa kịp thích nghi; vấn đề chính không phải giá vé hay ghế ngồi.

**Dẫn chứng trong transcript** (lượt T07, T08, T09): “Your route notes mention a problem before the textile gallery. Was the corridor too narrow? The main issue was the lighting transition. Visitors leave a bright space and enter a darker one almost immediately, with no time for their eyes to adjust. That could affect navigation even when signs are large enough. We should look at lighting and wayfinding together.”

**Phân tích phương án nhiễu:** **B** (ticket price) không phải thông tin/kết luận cuối phù hợp với yêu cầu câu hỏi; **C** (lack of seating) cũng không được đoạn trích xác nhận là đáp án. So sánh mục tiêu hỏi với kết luận và điều kiện trong lời thoại, không chỉ tìm từ trùng.

**Kỹ năng:** nghe paraphrase, kiểm tra kết luận và loại phương án được nhắc tới nhưng không đúng mục tiêu.

parts.title: Salt and the Weathering of Historic Stone

turns.text_en: A pale crust on a historic wall may look like an easy cleaning job. Yet removing it without understanding where it came from can make the damage worse. Today we'll follow water as it carries dissolved salts through porous stone, and see why drying conditions matter. I'll also distinguish what conservation teams can diagnose from what they can confidently promise to prevent.

Many masonry materials are examples of porous stone, containing networks of tiny spaces into which water can move. The size and connectivity of these pores influence what happens next. A stone with a smooth outer face may still absorb moisture through joints or cracks. Observing a wet patch alone does not reveal the full route the water has taken, so building surveys examine materials and structural details together.

Groundwater can carry dissolved salts into a building through foundations and lower walls. However, it is rarely wise to assume that every damp wall has exactly that source. Leaking roofs, blocked gutters and rain driven by the wind can all contribute moisture. Conservators map the pattern of dampness and look for evidence that distinguishes the possible pathways before recommending an intervention.

As water reaches a warmer or drier surface, evaporation removes the liquid while leaving many dissolved substances behind. Salts can then accumulate near the zone where moisture repeatedly arrives and disappears. The location of that zone may shift with season and building use. A salt deposit is thus evidence of movement, not simply dirt that appeared without a physical process.

The formation of salt crystals is called crystallisation. Under certain conditions, crystals grow inside small pores and exert pressure on the surrounding material. Repeated wetting and drying can make damage worse, although the behaviour depends on the particular salt and the environment. This mechanism explains why washing a wall carelessly may relocate the problem rather than remove its cause.

A common visible symptom is surface flaking, where thin sheets or grains detach from the stone. Similar-looking damage can have different causes, including frost or inappropriate repair materials. A good survey therefore combines visual observations with information about moisture and salts. Conservators avoid taking large destructive samples when a smaller, targeted investigation can answer the relevant question.

The relative humidity of indoor air influences the moisture balance of porous materials. Some salts absorb water from humid air, which may allow repeated changes even without obvious rainfall. A conservation plan may include monitoring indoor conditions before installing new heating or ventilation. Abrupt changes to a historic environment can create fresh stresses, so control measures are introduced cautiously and evaluated over time.

One possible treatment is desalination, a process intended to reduce soluble salts in vulnerable material. It may involve carefully selected absorbent poultices, but the treatment must be tested because it can also move moisture and damage delicate surfaces. There is rarely a simple one-day cure. Conservators usually combine limited interventions with monitoring to see whether the underlying source of water has changed.

Repairs should use materials compatible with the original masonry. In some historic buildings, lime mortar allows different moisture movement from a dense modern cement mix. This does not mean lime is automatically right in every case, but it illustrates why a repair material's properties must be considered. A very hard patch may force moisture into adjacent, weaker stone and make the overall damage worse.

Long-term monitoring provides the evidence needed to judge whether repairs are working. Teams may record photographs from fixed positions, moisture measurements and changes in visible salts across seasons. Without repeated observations, a building that looks improved immediately after cleaning could be deteriorating again. The results should be stored with dates and methods so future conservators can compare them reliably.

Sometimes the most effective action is to improve drainage around the building so less unwanted water reaches the foundations. Clearing a blocked channel may achieve more than repeatedly treating the same stained wall. Yet drainage work can affect archaeology and neighbouring structures, so it must be planned with specialists. The objective is to reduce harmful moisture pathways while protecting the historic fabric and the context around it.

The important decision is therefore not simply which cleaner to buy. Conservators must establish where moisture enters, which salts are present and whether a treatment changes the way the wall dries. They may need to monitor the building after intervention. A good outcome isn't always a spotless surface; sometimes it's a stable one that retains its historical material.
